title: Early Cheras
capsule: The early Chera dynasty was one of the three ancient Tamil kingdoms of south India — alongside the Cholas and Pandyas — ruling territories corresponding broadly to modern Kerala and western Tamil Nadu from roughly the third century BCE, with their inland capital at Vanchi-Karuvur (modern Karur) and key ports at Muziris and Thondi on the Malabar Coast. Their most celebrated ruler, Chenguttuvan ('the Red-Eyed Chera'), is lauded in Sangam poetry and the epic Cilappatikāram for northern campaigns and establishing the cult of Kannagi; Pliny the Elder recorded the drain of Roman silver and gold into Kerala for black pepper traded through Chera ports. Chera power dissolved between the third and fifth centuries CE as the Kalabhra interregnum disrupted Tamil polities; no continuous successor dynasty emerged until the Kulasekharas claimed Chera lineage centuries later.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Sangam-era Chera territory is reconstructed from poetry and later chronicles with no administrative records surviving; the boundaries are highly approximate and the chronology of specific rulers remains actively debated among historians.
